facts.statement: Sphenacanthus lived approximately 359 million years ago and is considered one of the earliest members of the elasmobranch lineage leading to modern sharks.
facts.quote: It lived 359 million years ago, and probably it was one of the first member of the elasmobranchians, the lineage that leads to the modern sharks.

facts.statement: Unlike modern sharks, Sphenacanthus inhabited fresh water lagoons and likely hunted small fish.
facts.quote: Sphenacanthus probably hunted small fishes and, unlike their modern-day relatives, it inhabited fresh water lagoons.

facts.statement: Sphenacanthus possessed seven fins, heterodont dentition, and relatively long, deep mandibles.
facts.quote: Sphenacanthus had seven fins, two in the upper part and five in the underside, and it had a heterodont dentition and mandibles relatively long and deeper.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence suggests Sphenacanthus was a relatively large shark, likely exceeding one meter in length when fully grown.
facts.quote: These suggest that it was a relatively large shark, probably well over one meter in length when fully grown.

facts.statement: Sphenacanthus was discovered in Carboniferous terrains in Scotland and the Paraná Basin in Brazil, inhabiting ancient fresh water systems.
facts.quote: Sphenacanthus was discovered in Carboniferous terrains of Scotland (Visén Oil Shale Groups), in the United Kingdom, in ancient fresh water systems, a habitat that also is known in the Paraná Basin in Brazil (Rio do Rasto Formation).

facts.statement: Findings from the Puertollano Basin in Spain suggest that Sphenacanthus also lived in zones of marine influence, such as brackish waters.
facts.quote: Another findings, like those of the Puertollano Bason in Spain suggests that also it lived in zones of marine influence, in brackish waters.

facts.statement: It is possible that Sphenacanthus preyed on its smaller relatives.
facts.quote: It is possible that Sphenacanthus may have preyed on its smaller relatives.

facts.statement: The genus Sphenacanthus was described by Agassiz in 1837.
The type species of the genus Sphenacanthus is Sphenacanthus serrulatus.
Sphenacanthus belongs to the family Sphenacanthidae.
Sphenacanthus is classified within the order Ctenacanthiformes.
Sphenacanthus is a member of the class Chondrichthyes.
Sphenacanthus belongs to the subclass Elasmobranchii.
Sphenacanthus is an animal within the kingdom Animalia.
Sphenacanthus belongs to the phylum Chordata.
There are 11 recorded fossil occurrences of the genus Sphenacanthus in the Paleobiology Database.
